supported.text: A and B are the better pair for looking at change over time: 2.7 days apart with matched wavelength (1.257 µm in both). They still differ in pointing, pipeline build and the PERSIST flag at the marker in B.

The dot that jumps between A and B is a single flagged pixel (NONFUNC, TRANSIENT, SUR_ERROR) at the same detector position in both frames. Its flags and one-pixel shape mean it should not be treated as a moving or new source. Its physical cause is not known from these data.
The dot only in A is flagged (TRANSIENT, OUTLIER, HALO, SUR_ERROR) and B and C show background there, so it gives no reason to claim a new object.
Among the features I checked, nothing supports a new or moving object between A and B.
The dot near the marker lines up with a catalogued Gaia field star (within about 1 arcsec), so it is not evidence of WISE 0855. The marker is a catalog prediction.
C has its own stretch, so its grey levels cannot be compared with A and B.
These images cannot show whether WISE 0855 moved: it is not identified in them and no position was measured.

not_supported.text: A new object appeared or something moved between A and B. The two dots that change are flagged pixels, and nothing about them supports a source in the sky.
The jumping dot was a cosmic ray, or any other specific cause. The flags say the pixel is unusable and a transient was detected; they do not establish what physically caused it.
Nothing at all changed in the sky. Only the bright features inspected here were checked, using display images and pipeline flags; that is not an exhaustive search.
The dot by the marker is WISE 0855. Its position matches a catalogued star, and position alone does not prove identity.
The marker shows where WISE 0855 was detected. The marker is a catalog prediction.
C's sky is brighter or dimmer than A's. C has its own stretch and a different wavelength, and no brightness was measured.
A and C show WISE 0855's motion. It is not identified in these frames and no position was fitted.
WISE 0855 is proven absent, or SPHEREx's detection limit here is known. Its faintness is an expectation from published measurements, not a measured non-detection or upper limit.

Different wavelengths or shifts smaller than a pixel can never be compared. They can, with a detected source, suitable data and a proper fit; these frames lack the detected source and no fit was made.
